summary: Considers how X.500 relates to Internet and UK domains. It is an Experimental document.

plainLanguage.summary: It asks how a big directory and Internet names could work together.

questions: how does x.500 relate to domains
how does x.500 relate to dns
what is a domaincomponent in x.500
can dns data be stored in x.500
subtitle: How the X.500 directory could sit above the Domain Name System, and how domain data could be stored in it.

tldr.problem: Internet domain names are short and flat in meaning, while the X.500 Directory offers longer, descriptive names and a richer information model. The RFC asks how the two naming worlds should relate.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes storing domains and RFC 822 mailboxes in the X.500 tree using new object classes and attributes, with DNS records kept as text, and linking the tree of descriptive names to the tree of domains by special attributes.
tldr.outcome: An Experimental proposal only. The author says there is no current intention to provide an operational replacement for DNS.

today: RFC 1279 is an Experimental RFC from November 1991, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself says there is no current intention to provide an operational replacement for DNS.

sections.title: Two Naming Systems
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) labels resources in a hierarchy, such as MIT.EDU or CS.UCL.AC.UK. Entries usually have one name, and information is attached to each entry as resource records. Name components tend to be short, such as CS. The local part of an RFC 822 mailbox can be seen as one level lower in the same hierarchy.

The OSI Directory, usually called X.500, is a very general naming framework. Its basic use is Organisationally Structured Names, where components tend to have longer values. One example is Country GB, Organisation University College London, Organisational Unit Computer Science, Common Name Stephen E. Hardcastle-Kille. The RFC calls this organisational X.500.
sections.plainLanguage: One system gives places short nicknames like CS. The other uses full, long names like Computer Science at University College London. Both are ways to find things.

sections.title: The Basic Model: A Layer Above Domains
sections.content:
The RFC quotes Paul Mockapetris: X.500 has as much relation to the DNS as DNS has to ARP. Organisational X.500 is a naming layer above domain names. Its values are longer and more descriptive, its tree is slightly shallower than the DNS tree, and it has a richer information framework.

From those differences the RFC concludes that two things should NOT be done: representing X.500 information in the DNS, and having an algorithmic mapping between the two hierarchies. Instead it proposes representing DNS information in the X.500 tree (the DIT) and giving the two parts of the tree a loose, weak linkage. It does not propose treating X.500 and domains as equivalent.

The RFC lists the possible benefits of putting domains in X.500: domain data reachable beyond MX records, remote management using X.500 security, user searching and browsing of the domain name space, room for extra management information such as who runs a system, mapping an RFC 822 mailbox to a Directory Name, and a place to attach certificates for privacy enhanced mail.
sections.plainLanguage: The big book should not copy the little book, and the two should not be forced to match line by line. Instead they just have sticky notes pointing at each other.

sections.title: Domains as Directory Entries
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new attribute, DomainComponent, and two new object classes. A Domain entry must contain a DomainComponent and may contain AssociatedName, organizationName, organizationalAttributeSet and manager. RFC822Mailbox is a subclass of Domain for mailboxes.

The mailbox S.Kille@cs.ucl.ac.uk becomes a chain of entries with DomainComponent values UK, AC, UCL, CS and finally S.Kille, the last one being of class RFC822Mailbox. The local part of a mailbox is thus treated as a special sort of domain component.

Wildcards are supported by using an asterisk as a special domain component name. A wildcard entry for two wildcard labels above PODUNK.COM is stored as two asterisk components above the remaining components. If a lookup of A.B.PODUNK.COM fails and reports two components matched, the client substitutes and looks up the wildcard entry explicitly.
sections.plainLanguage: Each part of an address, like UK then AC then UCL, becomes a folder inside the previous folder. A mailbox is just the last folder in the chain.

sections.title: Storing DNS Records
sections.content:
DNS information stored in the directory must be exactly equivalent to what is in the DNS, so the directory can be loaded from the DNS or the other way round. All authoritative records for a domain are stored. The directory does not emulate DNS caching or TTL handling, and master entries are assumed to be kept in step by DNS Zone Transfer or something equivalent.

The RFC considers three encodings for a record: ASN.1, the DNS binary format, and text. It chooses text, in IA5 characters, using the record syntax of section 5.1 of RFC 1035. The class and TTL may come in either order, the class defaults to IN, domains are always fully specified, and the TTL is always present. A DNSDomain object class holds a single DNSRecord attribute type, so new DNS record types need no new definitions, at the cost of the client doing the filtering. CNAME records map onto Directory Aliases.

A domain is looked up by translating it algorithmically to a Distinguished Name and reading the wanted attributes. Reverse information uses the usual IN-ADDR domain, represented the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of inventing a new secret code for each kind of note, the book just copies the notes in plain writing, so anyone can read them and copy them back.

sections.title: Networks and Linking the Two Trees
sections.content:
The RFC sketches a Network object class, with an IPNetwork subclass that must have an AssociatedDomain. A network such as UCL-Ethernet, University College London, GB would have two domains, 0.0.40.128.IN-ADDR.ARPA and UCL-ETHERNET.UCL.AC.UK, both represented in the tree, following the structures of RFC 1101.

Aliases are not suitable for linking the organisational tree to the domain tree, because a domain is not an organisation and a person is not a mailbox. So the RFC defines stronger links. An AssociatedDomain attribute on an organisation entry points into the DNS part, for example UCL.AC.UK for University College London, GB. An AssociatedName attribute on a domain entry points back to the organisational entry. The preferred setup keeps domain entries skeletal and avoids duplicating information. The example is 1:1, but a domain may relate to several organisations or the reverse.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry in one book carries a note saying where to look in the other book, so you can hop between the long name and the short one.

sections.title: Proposed Pilot and Security
sections.content:
The RFC calls for experiments in a pilot environment and describes a possible approach in an appendix. The tools it lists are a user lookup tool, a procedural library, a zone transfer tool between a DSA and a nameserver, a tool that patches in the reverse linkage pointers, a DNS manager tool, a mailbox download tool, and an emulation DNS server that uses the Directory as its database.

The first step is to use zone transfer to load a large part of the DNS into a single DSA and let pilot sites look up domain information. Later steps spread the data over several DSAs and finally master some parts of the DNS hierarchy in the directory.

On security, the memo does not directly address it, but says that because of X.500 facilities the proposal could lead to a more secure way to access and manage domain information.
sections.plainLanguage: Before changing anything for real, the author suggests a small test run: copy the nickname book into the big book, see if people like it, and only then think about going further.
